421.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable; making Zeal his bow, its string Carefulness in walking (iriyâ), and its top (where the string is fastened) Content, he should bend (this bow) with Truth, piercing with the arrow, Penance, (the foe's) mail, Karman--(in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Samsâra.”
421.explanation: Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, urges King Nami to build walls, gates and moats before renouncing; Nami answers that the sage's real fortress and weapons are inner virtues, guarded by the three guptis (control of mind, speech and body), with which he pierces the armour of karma.
421.tie_back: Like Valluvar, who calls wisdom both a weapon and an inner fortress no enemy can breach, Nami turns the king's walls and bow into inward qualities that cannot be besieged.
421._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (diacritic asterisks removed). The fortress-plus-weapon pairing matches the Kural's karuvi/aran image very closely, though Nami's 'fortress' is faith and self-control rather than discernment (arivu) as such.

422.quote_or_event: “The unruly, dreadful, bad horse, on which you sit, runs about, Gautama! how comes it to pass that it does not run off with you?” … “I govern it well in its course by the bridle of knowledge; it does not go astray with me, it keeps to the right path.” … “The mind is that unruly, dreadful, bad horse; I govern it by the discipline of the Law (so that it becomes a well-) trained Kambôga-steed.”
422.explanation: In the dialogue between Kesi (of Parshva's line) and Gautama (Mahavira's disciple), the mind is a runaway horse that knowledge reins in and keeps on the right path, until it becomes a well-trained steed.
422.tie_back: Valluvar defines wisdom as not letting the mind go wherever it wanders but leading it from evil to the good; Gautama's 'bridle of knowledge' does exactly that: it restrains the mind and steers it onto the right path.
422._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one: knowledge restrains the wandering mind and keeps it on the right path, matching both the restraining and the redirecting halves of the Kural.

423.quote_or_event: “Wisdom recognises the truth of the Law and the ascertainment of true things.”
423.explanation: The followers of Parshva and of Mahavira were troubled because the two teachers' rules differed (four vows against five, clothing against none). Gautama's answer is that wisdom looks past the outward differences to what is actually true, and Kesi, satisfied, accepts it.
423.tie_back: The Kural asks the wise to find the real substance (meipporul) of whatever is said by whoever says it; Gautama likewise tells the disputing disciples to judge by the truth of the matter, not by which master's label a rule carries.
423._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Good thematic fit, but the verse is about discerning the Law (dharma) behind differing rules, not a general maxim about weighing every speaker's claims. Jain anekantavada would also fit this Kural but is not quoted here.

424.quote_or_event: In the debate at Sravasti, the monk Kesi puts his questions to Gautama as riddles: a thousand foes attacking him, a poisonous plant in the heart, a raging fire, a runaway horse, a leaking boat. Each time Gautama grasps the hidden meaning and answers in plain, memorable words (the foe is the unsubdued self and the passions, the fire is the passions, the boat is the body), until Kesi and the whole assembly are satisfied.
424.explanation: The episode presents an ideal of communication on both sides: Gautama sees the subtle sense in what Kesi says and then gives that sense back in clear, simple terms that his hearers can take in.
424.tie_back: Valluvar's wise person both speaks so that the meaning easily sinks in and sees the subtle meaning in others' words; Gautama shows both skills, decoding Kesi's riddles and answering in a way the whole assembly can follow.
424._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of an episode read in full on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: the lecture models clear speech and subtle understanding without stating them as a teaching on communication. Jacobi's own note says Gautama 'at once understands the true meaning of the similes.'

425.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sûtras.” … “If he does not meet with a clever companion who surpasses or equals him in virtue, he should live by himself, abstaining from sins and not devoted to pleasures.”
425.explanation: The lecture on the causes of carelessness makes the company one keeps part of the road to liberation: serve worthy elders, avoid fools, and choose only a companion who equals or surpasses oneself in virtue, or else live alone.
425.tie_back: The Kural's first half says excellence lies in befriending the worthy of the world; the Jain text likewise makes association with the wise, and avoidance of fools, a deliberate discipline.
425._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong match for the first half (befriending the worthy); the Kural's second half, steadiness in friendship without blooming and closing, has no direct counterpart here.

426.quote_or_event: Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra opens its account of lay conduct with the qualities of the mārgānusārī, the householder who is 'following the path' even before taking the vows. Among them are earning wealth honestly and conforming to the proper, approved customs of one's society and country.
426.explanation: For Jain teachers, a layperson's spiritual path begins with being a decent and well-adjusted member of society, living by the accepted good customs around them, before any higher discipline is taken up.
426.tie_back: Valluvar's wisdom of 'living as the (worthy) world lives' corresponds to the Jain picture of the householder whose first virtues include fitting in with the sound customs of his land.
426.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, ch. 1 (the mārgānusārī qualities of the householder); paraphrased
426._accuracy_note: Next-best match. The list item on following approved social customs was confirmed only from a search summary of a jainworld.com page that would not load, so it is paraphrased and no verse number is given. Canonical scripture has no clear maxim on conforming to the world, and monastic texts stress renouncing it.

427.quote_or_event: “'If he does not get (victory over his will) early, he will get it afterwards;' such reasoning presupposes the eternity of human life. But such a man despairs when his life draws to its close, and the dissolution of his body approaches.”
427.explanation: Mahavira's discourse on carelessness mocks the man who keeps putting off self-conquest as if life will last forever. Such a person fails to see what is coming and is left in despair when death arrives.
427.tie_back: The Kural says the wise know beforehand what will come and the unwise cannot; the Jain verse gives the unwise person's typical mistake, reasoning as if the future will never arrive.
427._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Partial fit: the foresight here is specifically awareness of death and the urgency of spiritual effort, not the general practical judgment of consequences meant in the Porutpal context.

428.quote_or_event: “A monk should step carefully in his walk (i.e. in his life), supposing everything to be a snare for him.”
428.explanation: The Jain ideal of vigilance (apramāda) asks the aspirant to move through life as if surrounded by snares: an alert, well-placed caution toward what can bind the soul with karma, not panic.
428.tie_back: Valluvar calls it folly not to fear what should be feared; the Jain monk's habit of treating every step as a possible snare is exactly that wise fear of real dangers.
428._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: the verse teaches pervasive caution and does not contrast fearing the right things with the wrong ones as the Kural's chiasmus does, and the danger in view is spiritual (karmic bondage), not worldly.

429.quote_or_event: “He who is careless in all respects, is in danger; he who is not careless in all respects, is free from danger.” … “Faithful according to the commandment (of the Tîrthakaras), wise, and understanding the world according to the commandment--such a man is without danger from anywhere.”
429.explanation: The Acaranga teaches that constant vigilance, together with wisdom and a true understanding of the world, leaves a person without danger from any quarter; carelessness is what exposes one to danger.
429.tie_back: Valluvar promises that no calamity will shake those who guard in advance against what is coming; the Acaranga likewise says the vigilant and wise man is 'without danger from anywhere.'
429.source: Acaranga Sutra I.3.4.1, I.3.4.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
429._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit in structure. Jacobi's footnote explains the 'danger' as heaping up karma, so the protection meant is spiritual rather than against worldly calamity.

430.quote_or_event: “He who knows one thing, knows all things; and he who knows all things, knows one thing.”
430.explanation: Jacobi's note explains that true knowledge of any one thing cannot be separated from true knowledge of everything. In Jain thought the soul's own nature is knowledge, which reaches its completion in omniscience (kevala-jñāna).
430.tie_back: Valluvar says those who have wisdom have everything; the Acaranga makes a parallel claim about knowledge itself: whoever truly has it has, in principle, all of it.
430.source: Acaranga Sutra I.3.4.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
430._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: the Acaranga speaks of the unity of true knowledge (an epistemological and soteriological claim), while the Kural says wisdom is worth more than every other possession.
